group.title: People and description
group.blurb: Family, nationality, languages, and how to describe what someone looks like, including the adjective ending that decides whether it is een klein huis or een kleine man.

topics.title: Family
topics.summary: Every family word you need, the gezin versus familie split, and why neef can mean two completely different relatives.

blocks.title: gezin is not familie
blocks.body: `het gezin` is the people you live with, parents and children. `de familie` is everyone you are related to, including cousins in another country. Asking `Hoe groot is jouw gezin?` gets you a very different number from `Hoe groot is jouw familie?`.

rows: the male cousin or the nephew
the female cousin or the niece

blocks.title: neef and nicht are ambiguous
blocks.body: Dutch uses one word for cousin and for nephew or niece. If it matters, spell it out: `de zoon van mijn tante` (my cousin) or `de zoon van mijn broer` (my nephew).

Two prefixes do most of the work:
- `schoon-` marks family by marriage: `de schoonvader`, `de schoonmoeder`, `de schoonouders`, `de schoonzus`, `de schoondochter`
- `stief-` marks step-family: `de stiefvader`, `de stiefmoeder`, `het stiefkind`
Two words break the pattern: `de zwager` (brother-in-law) and `de halfbroer / de halfzus`.

Adding `-je` makes a word small, young or affectionate. It is called the `verkleinwoord` (the little form). Every word with `-je` becomes a **het-word**, whatever it was before.
- `de hond` gives `het hondje` (the little dog)
- `de neef` gives `het neefje` (the young cousin or nephew)
- `het huis` gives `het huisje` (the little house)
The ending has variants after certain sounds: `-tje` (het autootje), `-pje` (het boompje), `-kje` (het koninkje).

items.en: Do you have brothers or sisters?

items.nl: Ik heb twee broers en drie zussen.
items.en: I have two brothers and three sisters.

items.nl: Wie is ouder, jij of je zus?
items.en: Who is older, you or your sister?

items.nl: Ik ben de oudste. Mijn broer is de jongste.
items.en: I am the eldest. My brother is the youngest.

items.nl: Hoe heten je ouders en waar wonen ze?
items.en: What are your parents called and where do they live?

items.nl: Mijn moeder heet Dorine. Ze woont samen met mijn vader en hun hondje Sam.
items.en: My mother is called Dorine. She lives with my father and their little dog Sam.

blocks.title: Family riddles are the fastest drill
blocks.body: Build them with `van`: `Wie is de zus van je moeder?` (je tante), `Wie is de man van je oma?` (je opa), `Wie is de zoon van je broer?` (je neef). Ask a Dutch speaker a few and the vocabulary sticks in one evening.

key_takeaways: het gezin is parents plus children, de familie is every relative.
neef and nicht cover both cousin and nephew or niece, so use van to be precise.
schoon- marks in-laws, stief- marks step-family.
Any word ending in -je is small and always a het-word.

exercises.prompt: Wie is de zus van je moeder?
exercises.explain: Your mother's sister is your tante.

exercises.prompt: Wie is de man van je oma?
exercises.explain: Your grandmother's husband is your opa or grootvader.

exercises.prompt: Wie is de man van je zus?
exercises.explain: Your sister's husband is your zwager, one of the words that does not use schoon-.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks Hoe groot is jouw gezin? What are they asking about?
exercises.explain: het gezin is the household: parents and children. de familie is everyone else too.

exercises.prompt: Which article goes with hondje?
exercises.explain: Every -je word is a het-word, even when the original word took de.

exercises.prompt: Say you have no brothers or sisters.
exercises.explain: enig kind is the fixed expression for an only child.

exercises.prompt: Build the question: do you have brothers or sisters?
exercises.explain: Yes/no question, so the verb comes first, and hebt loses its t before je.

exercises.prompt: Your mother-in-law is:
exercises.explain: schoon- marks family by marriage, stief- marks step-family.

topics.title: Countries, nationalities and languages
topics.summary: One table you can read three ways, the four nationality endings, and the capital-letter rule that surprises almost everyone.

blocks.note: Read across: the nationality and the language are usually the same word. Brazil, the United States, Mexico and Morocco are the reminders that they are not always.

blocks.body:
Nationality words cluster into four endings. Knowing them lets you guess a country you have not learned yet.
- `-s`: Duits, Engels, Frans, Grieks, Turks, Pools, Japans
- `-isch`: Russisch, Somalisch, Georgisch
- `-aans`: Italiaans, Mexicaans, Amerikaans, Marokkaans, Indiaas
- `-ees`: Portugees, Chinees, Libanees

blocks.title: Capital letters, always
blocks.body: Dutch writes nationalities and languages with a **capital letter**, even in the middle of a sentence: `Ik spreek Nederlands en Engels.` Many languages do not do this, so it is an easy point to lose in writing.
`Nederlands` is the adjective and the language. The **person** is a different word, and it has a male and a female form.

items.nl: Wat is je nationaliteit? Ik ben Nederlands.
items.en: What is your nationality? I am Dutch.

items.note: the formal version, note the -e on Nederlandse

items.nl: Welke talen spreek je? Ik spreek Nederlands, Engels en Spaans.
items.en: Which languages do you speak? I speak Dutch, English and Spanish.

items.nl: Ik kom uit India, maar ik woon in Nederland.
items.en: I come from India, but I live in the Netherlands.

blocks.title: No article with a language
blocks.body: Say `Ik spreek Nederlands`, not `het Nederlands` in everyday speech. The article only appears in formal or technical phrasing: `Het Nederlands is een Germaanse taal.`

key_takeaways: Nationality and language are usually the same word, with Brazil, the US, Mexico and Morocco as the reminders that they are not.
Nationalities and languages always take a capital letter in Dutch.
The person is a separate word: een Nederlander, een Nederlandse.

exercises.prompt: Land: Duitsland. Wat is de taal?
exercises.explain: Duitsland gives Duits for both the nationality and the language.

exercises.prompt: Which language is spoken in Brazilië?
exercises.explain: The nationality is Braziliaans but the language is Portugees. Braziliaans is not a language.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence writes the language names correctly?
options: Ik spreek het nederlands en engels.
exercises.explain: Languages always take a capital letter in Dutch, and no article in everyday speech.

exercises.prompt: A man from the Netherlands is:
exercises.explain: The person word is een Nederlander. Nederlands is the adjective and the language.

exercises.prompt: Which nationality ending group does Russisch belong to?
exercises.explain: Russisch, Somalisch and Georgisch all take -isch.

exercises.prompt: Build the question: which languages do you speak?
exercises.explain: welke plus the noun comes first, then the verb, then the subject. spreekt loses its t before je.

exercises.prompt: Say you speak a little Dutch.
exercises.explain: een beetje plus the language name, capitalised in writing.

topics.title: Describing appearance
topics.summary: Three verbs do the whole job: you ARE tall, you HAVE brown eyes, and you WEAR glasses. Get those right and the vocabulary is easy.

rows: height, age, build, being bald or blond
Hij is lang. Zij is klein. Hij is kaal.
Zij heeft bruine ogen. Hij heeft een baard.
blocks.note: Glasses can take either verb: Hij heeft een bril and Hij draagt een bril are both fine.

items.nl: Mijn vader is lang. Hij heeft kort, bruin en steil haar.
items.en: My father is tall. He has short, brown, straight hair.

items.nl: Mijn moeder is klein. Ze heeft korte, bruine krullen.
items.en: My mother is short. She has short, brown curls.

items.nl: Mijn vader draagt een bril en mijn moeder draagt geen bril.
items.en: My father wears glasses and my mother does not wear glasses.

blocks.title: kort is not klein
blocks.body: `klein` is short in height, `kort` is short in length. A person is `klein`, but their hair is `kort`. Saying `Hij heeft klein haar` sounds like the hair itself is a small object.

rows: blond, bruin, zwart, rood, grijs, wit, geverfd
een staart, een knot, een vlecht, een pony

blocks.title: haar is singular, ogen is plural
blocks.body: `het haar` is one het-word with no article in a description, so it takes no -e: `Hij heeft **bruin** haar`. `de ogen` is plural, so the adjective always takes -e: `Hij heeft **bruine** ogen`. That single difference explains why the two sentences look inconsistent.

items.note: eruitzien splits, so eruit goes to the end

items.en: What colour hair does she have?
What colour eyes does he have?

items.nl: Heeft zij steil haar of krullen?
items.en: Does she have straight hair or curls?

blocks.title: The guessing game
blocks.body: Describing a face in yes/no questions is the fastest practice there is: `Heeft hij een baard?`, `Draagt zij een hoed?`, `Is het een vrouw?`, `Heeft hij dikke lippen?`. Every answer is `Ja` or `Nee`, so you can focus on the question form.

key_takeaways: zijn for height, age and being bald, hebben for hair and eyes, dragen for glasses and hats.
klein is short in height, kort is short in length.
bruin haar has no -e (het-word, no article), bruine ogen does (plural).
Hoe ziet hij eruit? sends eruit to the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence describes someone's eyes correctly?
exercises.explain: Eyes are something you have, and ogen is plural so the adjective takes -e.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Hij heeft ___ haar. (bruin)
exercises.explain: het haar is a singular het-word with no article here, so the adjective stays bare: bruin haar.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Mijn moeder ___ een bril.
exercises.explain: Glasses take dragen or hebben. Both are natural.

exercises.prompt: Your friend is 1.60 m tall. Which is right?
exercises.explain: klein is short in height. kort is for length, as in kort haar.

exercises.prompt: Build the question: what does she look like?
exercises.explain: eruitzien is a split verb, so eruit lands at the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Ask what colour eyes he has.
exercises.explain: Welke kleur ogen heeft hij? The noun sits right after welke kleur.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says he has no hair?
exercises.explain: kaal is a state, so it takes zijn: Hij is kaal.

exercises.prompt: Build: my mother has short, brown curls.
exercises.explain: krullen is plural, so both adjectives take -e: korte, bruine krullen.

topics.title: Adjective endings
topics.summary: Adjectives before a noun almost always take -e. There is exactly one situation where they do not, and this is how to spot it in a second.

blocks.body:
An adjective standing **before a noun** normally takes `-e`.
- `de grote man`, `een grote man`
- `de kleine huizen`, `kleine huizen`
- `mijn nieuwe fiets`, `dit lekkere eten`

blocks.title: No -e when all three are true
blocks.body:
Leave the `-e` off only when the noun is:
1. a **het-word**, and
2. **singular**, and
3. **indefinite** (after `een`, `geen`, or with no article at all)

That gives `een klein huis`, `geen groot probleem`, `lekker eten`. Change any one of those three and the -e comes back: `het kleine huis`, `kleine huizen`, `dit kleine huis`.

blocks.note: Only one cell in the whole table has no -e. That is the entire rule.

blocks.body:
Adding `-e` opens the last syllable, so the same sound rules kick in:
- long vowel loses a letter: `groot` gives `grote`, `duur` gives `dure`
- short vowel doubles the consonant: `dik` gives `dikke`, `wit` gives `witte`
- f goes back to v and s back to z: `lief` gives `lieve`, `grijs` gives `grijze`

rows: long o keeps one letter in an open syllable
short i needs the double consonant
short i needs the double consonant
f becomes v when it is no longer final
s becomes z when it is no longer final

blocks.body:
- Adjectives ending in `-en` take no `-e`: `een open deur`, `mijn eigen huis`, `een gouden ring`, `een tevreden klant`.
- After `zijn`, `worden` or `blijven` the adjective is **never** inflected, because it is not standing in front of a noun:
  - `Het huis is groot.`
  - `De man is groot.`
  - `Zij wordt moe.`

blocks.title: The most common learner slip
blocks.body: Saying `Het huis is grote`. Adjectives after `zijn` stay bare, always. The `-e` only appears when the adjective sits directly before its noun.

- `geen` negates a noun that has `een` or no article: `Ik heb **geen** bril.`, `Wij hebben **geen** kinderen.`
- `niet` negates everything else, and usually sits at the end or just before the word it targets: `Ik werk **niet**.`, `Hij is **niet** lang.`, `Dat is **niet** mijn fiets.`

items.en: My mother does not wear glasses.

items.nl: Wij hebben geen kinderen of huisdieren.
items.en: We have no children or pets.

items.nl: Hij is niet groot en niet klein.
items.en: He is neither tall nor short.
I do not understand the teacher.
items.note: definite noun, so niet, and it goes to the end

blocks.note: Comparison uses dan: Hij is groter dan zijn broer. The superlative takes de or het: Zij is de jongste.

key_takeaways: Before a noun, an adjective takes -e by default.
The only exception is a singular indefinite het-word: een klein huis.
After zijn, worden or blijven the adjective never takes an ending.
geen replaces een before a noun, niet negates everything else.

exercises.prompt: Complete with groot: een ___ huis.
exercises.explain: het huis, singular, after een, so no -e. All three conditions are met.

exercises.prompt: Complete with groot: het ___ huis.
exercises.explain: het makes it definite, so the -e comes back. Long o loses a letter: grote.

exercises.prompt: Complete with groot: een ___ man.
exercises.explain: de man is a de-word, so the -e always appears.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence gets the adjective ending right after zijn?
exercises.explain: After zijn the adjective is never inflected.

exercises.prompt: Complete with wit: een ___ muur. (de muur)
exercises.explain: de-word, so -e. The short i needs a doubled consonant: witte.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses geen correctly?
exercises.explain: geen replaces een before a noun. niet een is not used here.

exercises.prompt: Build: I do not understand the teacher.
exercises.explain: With a definite noun you use niet, and it goes to the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Complete with lief: een ___ man.
exercises.explain: de man takes -e, and the f goes back to v once it is no longer at the end: lieve.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase takes no -e?
exercises.explain: Adjectives ending in -en never inflect: een gouden ring, een open deur.
